records.content:
This Project Pythia Cookbook covers supervised machine learning readiness on a climate-model large ensemble: one classification
question — does the autumn ENSO state predict a wet Front Range winter? — answered on NSF NCAR’s own


CESM2 Large Ensemble (the AWS Open Data copy; no account, free egress),
walked along the analysis spine of NSF Unidata’s


Supervised Machine Learning Readiness, in seven short chapters.

This cookbook is for Earth system scientists, engineers and software staff who are new to machine learning, or who use it
without training. It assumes Python at the level of the 

Xarray tutorial and no ML. The seven chapters
take about 2 hours 35 minutes, and each runs on its own in under a minute from a committed table.

records.content:
The closest neighbour, in the ProjectPythia organisation though not yet listed in the gallery, is the 

Precipitation Machine Learning Cookbook, a short
scikit-learn introduction (regression on surface observations) that accompanies Unidata’s CyberTraining. The


CESM LENS on AWS Cookbook covers reading the CESM1 Large Ensemble, and the


scikit-learn Argo (also not yet listed), 

Landsat ML,


xbatcher ML and 

EO Data Science
cookbooks apply machine learning to other data. None yet walks a newcomer through a supervised classifier on a large ensemble,
where the members themselves are the unit the split has to respect.

So this cookbook changes exactly one of Unidata’s steps on purpose: the split is by ensemble member, and the forced response and the
wet threshold are fit on training members only. Chapter 3 measures what a member-blind split or a transform fitted before the split
would do to the score, rather than assuming it. Refinements are promoted on a paired test with a corrected standard error, and the result
is always read against the base rate of the same winters.

By the end you will be able to:

explain the steps of a supervised analysis (framing → data → split → train → validate → refine → test → justify) and name the failure each step guards against;

build and validate a classification model on a climate-model ensemble, reporting precision, recall and a confusion matrix;

compare refinement trials as a paired test across runs, so a gap inside the run-to-run spread is not read as a difference;

justify the chosen model honestly on measured performance and cost, including when nothing beats the base rate.

Seven chapters, each a notebook that runs on its own in a fresh kernel. Shared code lives in one file, notebooks/lensml.py, which

Chapter

What it does

01 Finding the data

the question as a decision; the intake-esm catalogue on AWS; the committed table

02 The target and the forced response

the forced response removed on training members only; one pooled “wet” threshold

03 Splitting by ensemble member

member-grouped folds; one model scored three ways to measure two leaks

04 Baselines and the ladder

three rules that fit nothing, then logistic, tree and boosting against the base rate

05 Refinement trials

the register, the corrected paired t-test, the Bonferroni line, a trial of your own

06 The held-out test, and the justification

the test, read against no skill and the cost of a false alarm; the limits

07 An out-of-period test

the same members’ SSP3-7.0 winters, scored once under a protocol fixed before the run

glossary. Two support files sit beside the chapters: cookbook-render.mjs, a MyST plugin that copies each

records.content:
The signal is weak. The straight-line relation between autumn Niño 3.4 and a wet winter is indistinguishable from zero. The final model,
gradient boosting at the base-rate threshold, shows a small precision edge on the held-out members, but that test is not blind: the
same 20 members were scored during development. Chapter 7 tests the edge on those members’ untouched SSP3-7.0 winters (2016–2100), under
a protocol written before that data was read (self-attested; it ships as notebooks/data/ssp370-test-protocol.md). The edge is not
confirmed: it does not replicate under the rule fixed before the run, but the test was small. A true edge of chapter 6’s size would
have cleared it only about 42% of the time (chapter 7 prints this), so the result gives no support for a briefing calling the winter
statistically wetter, and does not rule such an edge out. Chapter 6 states the limits: a
model-world study, on a ~1° grid, of total precipitation, in DJF, for a box that crosses the Divide.

As optional further material, 

ncar​-ml​-readiness​-course keeps the same data
and split and goes on to a small neural network; nothing in it is needed here.

Every parameter in lensml.py is a design decision with its reason; changing one is a trial you record. The seed is declared once and passed down — never np.random.seed() (scikit-learn’s Common pitfalls, §12.3.3).

The person who acts on the answer is the forecaster drafting a local winter-outlook briefing, such as NWS Boulder’s (September 2020) or
NWS Pueblo’s (2025). The official wet, dry or “equal chances” lean is the Climate Prediction Center’s; the briefing relays it and says what
the ENSO state suggests locally (Pueblo’s 2025 briefing does both). A “wet” call right more often than the base rate, without missing most
wet winters, would let the briefing say the ENSO state statistically favours a wet winter, beside CPC’s “equal chances” (Pueblo’s 2025 briefing:
“Statistically, warmer and drier SE CO, but CPC’s forecast is equal chances”). The figure draws the question’s two boxes from the parameters (no data, no coastlines).

def span(box):
    """A box as degrees with hemispheres, from its slices on the 0-360 grid."""

        return f"{abs(y):g}°{'S' if y < 0 else 'N'}"

        return f"{x:g}°E" if x <= 180 else f"{360 - x:g}°W"

    return f"{lat(y0)}–{lat(y1)}, {lon(x0)}–{lon(x1)}"

records.content:
Unidata opens every analysis with three questions, guarding against a target that answers no one’s decision.

Try it: frame it yourself first

Before opening the worked answers, write your own: three simple solutions a model must beat, whether the requirements can be met, and
the question as one decision.

The worked answers

Does a simpler solution exist? Three, and a model is measured against them, not assumed to beat them.

Simple solution

What it predicts

What it sets

always-dry

“dry” every winter

a bar on accuracy only (wet precision and recall are 0)

always-wet

“wet” every winter

recall 1 at precision = the base rate: the bar every precision is read against

Niño-sign rule

“wet” when the autumn Niño 3.4 anomaly is positive

the physical prior (NWS Boulder east of the Divide: El Niño wetter, La Niña drier); no bar

Can machine learning requirements be met? On the data side, yes: the catalogue holds monthly PRECC, PRECL and TS for every historical member in both forcing variants. On the physics side the honest prior is a small effect: Stagge et al. (2023) find the ENSO winter-precipitation signal over the Intermountain West is a north–south dipole, “the northern pole … north of 40° N” and “the southern pole … south of 35° N”, the Front Range, at about 38.5–40.5° N, between them; the northern pole’s sign is reversed (La Niña wetter). The signal is measured here, not assumed.

Which scientific question should be answered? “Given the autumn Niño 3.4 state in a CESM2 LENS member, will that member’s coming Front Range winter be wet — above the one pooled threshold that marks the upper third of the training members’ detrended winters?”

The catalogue forces two facts on the design: there is no monthly PRECT, so the target is PRECC + PRECL; and there is no variable named SST (and no ocean TEMP
for the historical-smbb half), so the Niño 3.4 index is built from atmospheric TS over open ocean.

Offline, each cell below prints OFFLINE and the chapter runs on from the cache. The second computes what a box subset reads.

CATALOG_URL = "https://ncar-cesm2-lens.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/catalogs/aws-cesm2-le.json"
try:
    cat = intake.open_esm_datastore(CATALOG_URL)
    subset = cat.search(
        component="atm",
        frequency="monthly",
        experiment="historical",
        variable=["PRECC", "PRECL", "TS"],
    )
    print(
        f"catalogue last_updated: {cat.esmcat.last_updated}   "
        f"rows in catalogue: {len(cat.df)}   rows selected: {len(subset.df)}"
    )
    cols = [
        "variable",
        "forcing_variant",
        "units",
        "start_time",
        "end_time",
        "path",
    ]
    with pd.option_context(
        "display.max_colwidth", None
    ):  # the six paths in full
        display(subset.df[cols])
except Exception as err:  # no network, a DNS failure, S3 unreachable
    if os.environ.get("CI"):  # CI has network: a failure there is real
        raise
    cat = subset = None
    print(
        f"OFFLINE: the catalogue at {CATALOG_URL} could not be read "
        f"({type(err).__name__}). The Metadata Document's catalogue and store "
        "rows are *not printed this run*; every later cell runs from the cache."
    )





try:
    probe = xr.open_zarr(
        "s3://ncar-cesm2-lens/atm/monthly/cesm2LE-historical-cmip6-TS.zarr",
        consolidated=True,
        storage_options={"anon": True},
    )
except Exception as err:  # offline: the structure rows are not printed
    if os.environ.get("CI"):  # CI has network: a failure there is real
        raise
    probe = None
    print(
        f"OFFLINE: the TS store could not be opened ({type(err).__name__}); "
        "the dims, calendar and chunking rows are *not printed this run*."
    )
if probe is not None:
    print("dims      :", dict(probe.sizes))
    print("coords    :", list(probe.coords))
    print(
        "members   :",
        probe.member_id.values[:3],
        "…",
        "calendar:",
        type(probe.time.values[0]).__name__,
    )
    ch = tuple(int(c) for c in probe["TS"].encoding["chunks"])
    per_chunk = (
        int(np.prod(ch)) * probe["TS"].dtype.itemsize
    )  # bytes, uncompressed
    n_time_chunks = -(
        -probe.sizes["time"] // ch[1]
    )  # chunks along time per member
    per_member_var = n_time_chunks * per_chunk
    n_members = (
        2 * probe.member_id.size
    )  # two halves, each the size of this store
    print(
        f"chunking  : {ch} {probe['TS'].dtype} → {per_chunk / 1e6:.0f} MB per chunk "
        f"uncompressed; one member-variable ({probe.sizes['time']} months) = "
        f"{n_time_chunks} chunks × {per_chunk / 1e6:.0f} MB ≈ {per_member_var / 1e6:.0f} "
        f"MB read for any box subset; the derivation ({n_members} members × 3 "
        f"variables) ≈ {n_members * 3 * per_member_var / 1e9:.0f} GB"
    )

Two box means for every member read the volume the chunking line computes, so the derivation runs once and writes data/member_winters.csv, which every chapter reads. Its reader asserts that the header records the current
SEASON, WINDOW, FRONT_RANGE, NINO34 and AUTUMN_MONTHS, and an access= date equal to ACCESS_DATE: a decision the cache
silently ignored would be a fit that cannot be rerun. One exception: the committed header predates the AUTUMN_MONTHS field, so the reader
assumes SON (the only autumn the code then had) and prints a line saying so. A rebuild records the field.

show(derive_member_winters, load_cache)



How a rebuild works. REBUILD = True below re-derives the table from S3 with the parameters in lensml.py. The full ensemble is a
background job (33 minutes on a fast link, 2026-10-20; an hour or more on home broadband); fewer members is a quick sample. A rebuild is a new access: it stamps its own date into the header, and the chapters then ask you to set ACCESS_DATE to match.

REBUILD = False  # True re-derives data/member_winters.csv from S3
N_MEMBERS_PER_HALF = (
    50  # used only when REBUILD = True; 50 = the full ensemble

The raw SON Niño 3.4 box mean and the winter precipitation both carry a forced trend (Rodgers et al. 2021 §3.1, Mean state changes; the check below prints
each one’s correlation with year). A degree-FORCED_DEG polynomial in year, fit to the training-member ensemble mean, is subtracted from
every member alike, leaving each member’s own departure from the shared path — the ENSO state, not the decade. Without it, the models would
learn time-of-century and it would read as ENSO skill.

Then the target: wet = 1 when the detrended precipitation sits above the WET_QUANTILE of the pooled training members. One
threshold for every member: a per-member quantile would fix each member’s base rate by construction, and the per-half check below could
never fail. Curve and threshold are transforms fit on training members and applied to everyone else — as a StandardScaler inside a
Pipeline is (scikit-learn’s Common pitfalls, §12.2.1) — written as two functions so that every validation fold in chapters 3–5 refits
them. One curve is fit to both forcing halves together; the per-half base-rate check below supports pooling them,
though it cannot see every difference a forcing half could make (chapter 6, limit 6).

show(fit_transforms, apply_transforms)



TRANSFORMS = fit_transforms(table[is_train])  # fit on ALL training members

records.content:
A forced path the curve missed (too low a degree, a mid-century bump) survives the subtraction as decades whose mean anomaly sits away
from zero. Each decade’s mean anomaly over the training members is divided by its standard error; the removal passes only if every
decade of both series lies within ±DECADE_TOL standard errors. The correlation of the anomaly with year is not used: it is zero by
construction for any FORCED_DEG >= 1, so it could never fail. The last line prints the chance that a correct removal trips the tolerance
somewhere by luck.

DECADE_TOL = 3.0
d = table[is_train]
decade = (d["winter"] // 10) * 10
for anom, raw in ANOMALIES.items():
    r = d[raw].corr(d["winter"])
    print(
        f"corr({raw:20s}, year) = {r:+.3f}   "
        "(the forced trend in the raw series, training members)"
    )
removal_ok, n_tests = True, 0
for anom in ANOMALIES:
    g = d.groupby(decade)[anom]
    z = g.mean() / (d[anom].std() / np.sqrt(g.size()))
    worst = z.abs().idxmax()
    ok = bool((z.abs() <= DECADE_TOL).all())
    removal_ok &= ok
    n_tests += len(z)
    print(
        f"{anom:12s} decade-mean anomaly in standard errors: worst {z[worst]:+.2f} "
        f"(the {worst}s) · tolerance ±{DECADE_TOL:.0f} → {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}"
    )
false_alarm = 1 - (1 - 2 * norm.sf(DECADE_TOL)) ** n_tests
verdict = (
    "PASS"
    if removal_ok
    else "FAIL — a forced path survived; change FORCED_DEG"
)
print(
    f"forced-response removal: {verdict}   ({n_tests} decade means; chance a "
    f"correct removal trips the tolerance somewhere ≈ {false_alarm:.0%})"
)

records.content:
scikit-learn’s guidance on grouped cross-validation: “all the samples in the validation fold come from groups that are not represented at
all in the paired training fold.” Three reasons make the member the group:

The question is about members never seen. The score has to come from a realisation the model has not met; a member-blind split
scores new years of members it already knows.

The transforms. The forced curve and the wet threshold are refit on each fold’s training members (score_splits calls
fit_transforms per fold). Fit before the split, held-out winters would help fit the curve and threshold that label them — the same
leak as a StandardScaler fit on the whole table.

Dependence is measured, not assumed. Rodgers et al. 2021 §2.2 is why WINDOW starts late, but they give no figure for how much
initial-condition memory is left after fifty years. The next cell prints the lag-1 autocorrelation inside each member, then the
correlation between micro-siblings (members sharing a start year, as the CESM2 LE project page defines them — the i1231-style token
in member_id) and between unrelated members, with a line that fails if siblings share more. Siblings are not grouped in the
split; that line is what licenses it.

Two splits are made, both by member, both from the declared seed: the test members (chapter 2) and member-grouped folds over the
rest, N_FOLDS = min(N_FOLDS_MAX, training members). The folds are stratified on the all-training labels, which decide only which members
share a fold; the labels scored inside a fold are refit on that fold’s training members.

show(member_folds)



N_FOLDS = S.n_folds
print(
    f"base rate train {train.wet.mean():.3f}   (the test members' base rate is "
    "printed once, in chapter 6; nothing here reads their labels)"
)
print(
    f"N_FOLDS = min(N_FOLDS_MAX={N_FOLDS_MAX}, {S.n_train_members} training "
    f"members) = {N_FOLDS}"
)
for k, (a, b) in enumerate(
    member_folds(RNG_SEED, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr)
):
    assert not set(g_tr[a]) & set(g_tr[b]), f"fold {k} leaks members"
print(
    f"{N_FOLDS} member-grouped folds verified: no member appears in both the "
    "fitting and the scoring side of any fold"
)
if S.n_repeats_effective == 1:
    print(
        f"NOTE: leave-one-member-out; the trials use 1 fold draw, not {N_REPEATS}"
    )


def lag1(s):
    v = np.asarray(s, dtype=float)
    return float(np.corrcoef(v[:-1], v[1:])[0, 1])


dependence = (
    train.groupby("member_id")
    .agg(lag1_nino34_anom=("nino34_anom", lag1), lag1_wet=("wet", lag1))
    .round(3)
)
print(
    "\nlag-1 autocorrelation within training members (what consecutive winters "
    "of one member share):"
)
print(dependence.to_string())
print("mean:", dependence.mean().round(3).to_dict())

MICRO_STARTS = {"1231", "1251", "1281", "1301"}
start_year = {
    m: re.search(r"i(\d{4})p", m).group(1) for m in train.member_id.unique()
}
print(
    f"\ncorrelation between training members over {WINDOW[0]}–{WINDOW[1]} "
    "(micro-siblings share a start year; the memory check):"
)
for anom in ANOMALIES:
    wide = train.pivot(index="winter", columns="member_id", values=anom)
    corr = wide.corr()
    sib, unrel = [], []
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(wide.columns, 2):
        same = start_year[a] == start_year[b] and start_year[a] in MICRO_STARTS
        (sib if same else unrel).append(corr.loc[a, b])
    sib, unrel = np.array(sib), np.array(unrel)
    if len(sib) < 2 or len(unrel) < 2:
        print(f"{anom:12s} too few member pairs of one kind to compare")
        continue
    excess = sib.mean() - unrel.mean()
    se = np.sqrt(sib.var(ddof=1) / len(sib) + unrel.var(ddof=1) / len(unrel))
    if abs(excess) <= 2 * se:
        reading = (
            "PASS: no sibling excess detectable (|excess| ≤ 2 SE, SE a lower "
            "bound) — the member is taken as the unit"
        )
    else:
        reading = (
            "FAIL: siblings still move together — group the folds by start "
            "year, or start WINDOW later"
        )

One function scores every validation run in this cookbook. With refit_transforms=True it refits the forced curve and wet threshold on each
fold’s training rows; with False it uses the columns fit once on all training members, before the folds.

show(score_splits)



Arm

Split unit

Forced curve and wet threshold fit on

A held-out score measures

A — this cookbook’s pipeline

member

that fold’s training members (refit in every fold)

new members

B — transforms fit before the split

member

all training members, before the folds

new members, scored with transforms they helped fit

C — member-blind split

winter (StratifiedKFold)

that fold’s training winters

new years of members the model already knows

B differs from A only in where the transforms are fit; C differs from A only in the split unit. The model is gradient boosting (chapter 4)
at the base-rate decision threshold, so that it calls wet. The cell’s first line scores the same model at scikit-learn’s default 0.5 and
prints how rarely it calls wet there: a precision resting on a handful of calls makes any gap a non-test, so below one wet call per hundred
winters the cell marks the gaps NON-TEST. Each arm prints its scores with per-fold SDs and its wet-call count, then its gaps against A
with the SD of the per-fold gaps — a rough scale; chapter 5’s paired test is the measurement.

Note what this cell is, for chapter 5: a validation score for boosting at the base-rate threshold, on the same seeds chapter 5 uses. Once
it has been read, a trial of that model is no longer a blind one.

CONTRAST_THRESHOLD = 1 - WET_QUANTILE  # the designed base rate
MIN_WET_CALL_SHARE = (
    0.01  # below this, precision and recall gaps are a NON-TEST
)


def contrast_model(seed):
    return FixedThresholdClassifier(
        GradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING_SETTINGS, random_state=seed),
        threshold=CONTRAST_THRESHOLD,
        response_method="predict_proba",
    )


arms = {
    "A member split, transforms refit in each fold   ": dict(
        runs=[], cm=np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    ),
    "B member split, transforms fit before the split ": dict(
        runs=[], cm=np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    ),
    "C member-blind split, transforms refit in fold  ": dict(
        runs=[], cm=np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    ),
}
_s05, _cm05 = score_splits(
    GradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING_SETTINGS, random_state=RNG_SEED),
    train,
    list(member_folds(RNG_SEED, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr)),
    refit_transforms=True,
)
print(
    f"for reference — the same model at sklearn's default threshold 0.5 (arm A's "
    f"split, one fold draw): wet calls {int(_cm05[:, 1].sum())} of {int(_cm05.sum())} "
    f"scored winters ({_cm05[:, 1].sum() / _cm05.sum():.2%}), recall "
    f"{_s05['recall'].mean():.3f} — too few calls to read a gap in"
)
for rep in range(S.n_repeats_effective):
    seed = RNG_SEED + rep
    by_member = list(member_folds(seed, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr))
    shuffled = StratifiedKFold(
        n_splits=N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=seed
    )
    by_year = list(
        shuffled.split(X_tr, y_tr)
    )  # member-blind: winters shuffled
    plan = [(by_member, True), (by_member, False), (by_year, True)]
    for (label, store), (splits, refit) in zip(arms.items(), plan):
        s, cm = score_splits(
            contrast_model(seed), train, splits, refit_transforms=refit
        )
        store["runs"].append(s)
        store["cm"] += cm
METRICS = ["ap", "precision", "recall", "accuracy"]
pooled_arm = {
    label: {m: np.concatenate([s[m] for s in st["runs"]]) for m in METRICS}
    for label, st in arms.items()
}
ref = pooled_arm[next(iter(pooled_arm))]


def sd(v):
    return v.std(ddof=1) if len(v) > 1 else 0.0


print(
    f"boosting at threshold {CONTRAST_THRESHOLD:.3f} (the base rate; 0.5 is sklearn's "
    f"default), {S.n_repeats_effective} fold draw(s) × {N_FOLDS} folds per arm. Per arm: "
    "scores (mean ± per-fold SD) and wet calls; then gap = arm − A (mean ± SD of the "
    "per-fold gaps)"
)
for label, s in pooled_arm.items():
    cm = arms[label]["cm"]
    wet_calls, n_scored = int(cm[:, 1].sum()), int(cm.sum())
    share = wet_calls / n_scored
    print(
        f"{label} AP {s['ap'].mean():.3f}   precision {s['precision'].mean():.3f} ± "
        f"{sd(s['precision']):.3f}   recall {s['recall'].mean():.3f} ± "
        f"{sd(s['recall']):.3f}   accuracy {s['accuracy'].mean():.3f}   wet calls "
        f"{wet_calls} of {n_scored} scored winters ({share:.1%})"
    )
    gaps = {m: s[m] - ref[m] for m in ["ap", "precision", "recall"]}
    if share >= MIN_WET_CALL_SHARE:
        reading = (
            f"gaps readable (wet calls ≥ {MIN_WET_CALL_SHARE:.0%} of winters)"
        )
    else:
        reading = "precision/recall gaps a NON-TEST: read AP only"
    print(
        f"{'':{len(label)}} gap vs A: AP {gaps['ap'].mean():+.4f} ± {sd(gaps['ap']):.4f}"
        f"   precision {gaps['precision'].mean():+.4f} ± {sd(gaps['precision']):.4f}   "
        f"recall {gaps['recall'].mean():+.4f} ± {sd(gaps['recall']):.4f}   → {reading}"
    )

records.content:
Read each arm’s gap vs A line against the SD printed beside it. On this table the leaks barely bite, for three reasons the printed lines
show:

No within-member persistence to memorise. The mean: line under the lag-1 table gives lag1_wet near zero: one wet winter says
almost nothing about the next in the same member, so a member-blind split (arm C) has little to learn from a member’s other years. The
input’s lag-1 is negative, not positive — no run of similar autumns either.

The input carries no member identity. With one detrended Niño 3.4 value per winter, nothing in a row tells the model which member it
came from, so it cannot memorise a member even when it has seen one.

The transforms are smooth fits to many members. A cubic in year through the mean of many training members, and one pooled quantile,
barely move when one fold’s members are left out — so fitting them before the split (arm B) leaks almost nothing.

A small gap here is a measurement on this design, not a licence: with a member-specific input (a member’s own past winters, say) or
transforms fit on fewer members, the same cell is where a member split earns its keep.

records.content:
Unidata’s instruction is to run trials “until … they no longer improve”. Improvement is judged against the run-to-run spread: each
trial repeats the member-grouped folds N_REPEATS times with different fold draws, and both models are scored on identical draws. Scores
from overlapping training sets are not independent, so a plain paired t-test under-estimates the variance. This cookbook uses the
Nadeau–Bengio corrected paired t-test, from scikit-learn’s example Statistical comparison of models using grid search
(BSD-3-Clause, credited in lensml.py).

“Corrected” means the standard error, not multiplicity. A plain paired t-test divides the variance of the k per-fold
differences by k; corrected_std multiplies it by 1/k + n_test/n_train instead, to account for the overlap between training sets;
it does nothing about running many tests. The test is one-sided: a candidate must
beat the incumbent, so a loss prints p near 1 (a change from the example, which took the absolute value under a right-tailed label).
The register prints _sd, the plain per-fold SD of the differences, for scale; _t divides the gap by the corrected error, and _t is
the test.

records.content:
Recall alone rewards calling wet always; precision alone rewards calling it almost never; AP cannot see a threshold. So a candidate is
promoted only if one of the two numbers the decision uses improves measurably — p < 0.05 with a positive gap — while the other does not
fall on average (mean gap ≥ 0). Both tests sit in every register row, with the wet-call share (called_wet_cand, called_wet_inc)
beside recall.

The example warns that “if multiple models are statistically compared, a multiple comparisons correction is needed when using the frequentist approach”. The register does
not apply one — each p is per test, uncorrected — so it bounds the looks at MAX_TESTED_TRIALS rows, two metrics each, and prints the
Bonferroni line (0.05 ÷ the looks so far) under every register. A p under 0.05 but above that line is a promotion under the
uncorrected rule only. The line counts only the register’s own looks: not chapter 3’s three contrast arms, not chapter 4’s table and
threshold rows, not any look you take outside this register.

What the rule cannot see. It compares a candidate with the incumbent only, and the first incumbent is the sign rule. If the sign
rule’s precision sits below the always-wet bar (chapter 4), a candidate with no skill at all — precision merely at the base rate — can
beat it. Read such a promotion as a promotion over the sign rule, not as skill; chapter 6 reads the tested model against the base rate of

        f"base rate / (1 − base rate) = {base / (1 - base):.2f}"

robust evaluation.”

Start from the cost chapter 4 named: a false alarm puts “statistically wetter” in a briefing before a dry winter, the costlier
error. The false alarms per hit line follows from precision alone: false alarms per hit = (1 − precision) / precision, so any model with precision below 0.5 makes

over always-wet on this question. An office that weighs a false alarm as heavily as a hit should leave the briefing at CPC’s “equal chances”. The precision edge
over the base rate is small (the interval line) and provisional (the test members were scored during development), and chapter 7’s test does not replicate it.

records.content:
The edge does not replicate under the rule fixed before the run. The PRIMARY OUTCOME line is the result: on the test members’
future winters, boosting at the base-rate threshold has a precision whose 95% interval over test members includes zero. The line after
the secondary outcomes shows the interval also includes chapter 6’s estimate, so this test cannot separate no edge from an edge of that size; the
outside the protocol line puts a number on how small the test was. It gives no support for a briefing calling the winter statistically wetter.

The secondary outcomes say the same from other sides. AP, which reads the ranking at every threshold, is not distinguishable from no skill
for the final model either (its AP − base rate line above). No comparator clears the base rate on precision (the comparator lines printed under the primary outcome): the Niño-sign rule and logistic at the base-rate threshold
sit inside the no-skill band, and always-wet sits on it by construction; always-dry calls nothing wet, so its precision is undefined
(scored 0). Every model that calls wet makes more
false alarms than hits (the false alarms per hit values), as precision below 0.5 must. The decile table’s chi-square line says whether
the wet rate differs between the training bins on these winters; read it beside chapter 2’s and chapter 6’s — the coldest bin is the
driest here, as in chapter 2, while in chapter 6’s test members the warmest was slightly drier; the omnibus test does not reject chance.

What this does not say: it does not show the historical edge was an artefact — a shift in period and forcing could hide a real but
fragile relation (limit 1). It does say that the chapter 6 edge, chosen after its validation score was seen and scored on members already
used, is not evidence a forecaster could lean on.

Glossary

records.content:
The terms the chapters use, in the sense they use them.

Term

Meaning here

ENSO, Niño 3.4

El Niño–Southern Oscillation; the Niño 3.4 index is the mean surface temperature over 5°S–5°N, 170°–120°W, the input here

SON, DJF

September–October–November (the autumn input) and December–January–February (the winter target)

forced response

the warming path every ensemble member shares by calendar year; removed so a model reads ENSO, not the decade

precision

of the winters a model calls wet, the share that were wet

recall

of the winters that were wet, the share the model called wet

AP (average precision)

precision averaged over every threshold of the model’s ranking; a ranking with no skill scores the base rate

base rate

the share of winters that are wet; a classifier with no skill has precision equal to it

wet-call share

the share of winters a classifier calls wet; a classifier with no skill has recall equal to it

ladder, rung

the candidate models in order of flexibility: rung 0 is three rules that fit nothing, rungs 1–3 are logistic regression, a decision tree and gradient boosting

trial

one recorded change, scored against the incumbent on the same folds

incumbent

the model currently ahead; a trial replaces it only if the promotion rule says so

register

the table of every trial, its paired-test results and its verdict

looks

the tests taken so far: two (recall, precision) per register row

Bonferroni line

0.05 divided by the looks; a p below 0.05 but above it is a promotion under the uncorrected rule only
